title: Migraine: Match Acute Therapy and Prevention to Disability, Risk, and Frequency
bottomLine: Typical recurrent migraine with a normal neurologic examination is usually a clinical diagnosis. Treat acute attacks early with an evidence-based strategy matched to severity and contraindications, prevent attacks when disability/frequency or acute-medication burden justifies it, and actively prevent medication-overuse headache.
recognize: Migraine often causes moderate-severe recurrent headache with nausea and/or photophobia/phonophobia and activity aggravation; aura is usually fully reversible and evolves over minutes.
Chronic migraine and frequent acute-medication use should trigger a preventive-strategy review.
differentiate: Thunderclap headache, new focal deficit, papilledema, fever/meningismus, pregnancy/postpartum severe headache, cancer/immunocompromise or major pattern change requires a secondary-headache pathway.
Cluster headache and tension-type headache have different clinical patterns and treatment strategies.
assessment: Document monthly headache and migraine days, disability, aura, acute-medication days, cardiovascular risk, pregnancy plans, sleep, mood and previous treatment response.
workup: Do not routinely image a stable episodic migraine with normal examination and no secondary red flags.
Use imaging/labs only when the secondary differential or atypical course requires them.
management: Use simple analgesics/NSAIDs or migraine-specific acute therapy such as triptans/gepants according to severity, prior response and contraindications.

Offer prevention when attack burden, disability, chronic migraine or medication overuse warrants it; current Canadian options include established oral preventives, onabotulinumtoxinA for appropriate chronic migraine and Health-Canada-approved CGRP-targeting therapies.
Combine medication with sleep/activity/meal regularity and trigger management without implying lifestyle caused migraine.
medicationSafety: Avoid vasoconstrictive triptans in relevant vascular contraindications and review pregnancy-specific choices.
Frequent acute analgesic/triptan use can perpetuate medication-overuse headache; preventive treatment is often safer than escalating rescue frequency.
counselling: Use a headache diary and set a clear acute-treatment and rescue plan, including limits that reduce medication overuse.
followUp: Reassess headache days, disability, acute-medication use and preventive tolerability after an adequate therapeutic trial.
examTrap: Ordering CT/MRI for every classic migraine—or repeatedly adding acute rescue drugs while ignoring medication-overuse and prevention needs.
oneLinePearl: Treat the attack early, prevent disability, and count acute-medication days.
sourceBasis: Canadian Headache Society 2024 Updated Migraine Prevention Guideline
Canadian Headache Society acute treatment guidance

title: Neuroimaging: Choose the Modality for the Clinical Question
bottomLine: Neuroimaging is useful when the result can answer a focused structural/vascular question and change care. CT is fast and strong for acute hemorrhage/trauma and selected emergencies; MRI is more sensitive for many parenchymal, posterior-fossa, demyelinating and subtle structural lesions; vascular imaging answers arterial/venous questions. Do not image routine uncomplicated syndromes just because a scan is available.
recognize: Acute stroke, head trauma, thunderclap headache, focal progressive deficits, suspected cord compression and raised-intracranial-pressure syndromes are examples where imaging may be time-critical.
Typical migraine, uncomplicated syncope, established epilepsy without new concerning features and uncomplicated early radiculopathy often do not require routine imaging.
differentiate: Noncontrast CT and MRI answer different questions; a normal CT can miss early ischemia/posterior-fossa disease.
CTA/MRA/MRV/CTV are vascular studies and should be chosen for suspected arterial occlusion/dissection/aneurysm or venous thrombosis rather than ordered reflexively.
assessment: Define onset/tempo, focal findings, trauma, anticoagulation, cancer/immunocompromise, infection, pregnancy, implanted devices and renal/contrast context before choosing imaging.
workup: Choose the least invasive modality that can answer the urgent question without delaying treatment.
Review contraindications/artifact issues and whether contrast changes diagnostic yield; pregnancy imaging uses risk-benefit and radiation/contrast principles rather than blanket avoidance.
management: Act on urgent findings through stroke, neurosurgical, infectious or spinal pathways.
For incidental/nonurgent abnormalities, avoid overdiagnosis by correlating imaging with the clinical syndrome.
medicationSafety: Contrast risks vary by agent and patient; current radiology policy governs renal/allergy/pregnancy decisions.
Sedation for imaging adds airway/delirium risk and should be used only when necessary.
counselling: Explain what the scan can answer and why an incidental finding may not explain symptoms.
followUp: Ensure critical/incidental results have an assigned owner and follow-up plan rather than simply documenting that imaging was ordered.
examTrap: Ordering a brain MRI for uncomplicated vasovagal syncope or typical migraine with a normal neurologic exam.
oneLinePearl: Image the question, not the anxiety.
sourceBasis: Canadian Stroke Best Practices imaging pathways

title: Neuromuscular Junction Disorders: Fatigability, Facilitation, Autonomic Clues, and Toxins
bottomLine: Neuromuscular-junction disorders cause weakness without a primary sensory level. Use the pattern to separate myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, botulism and medication/toxin effects, and treat respiratory/bulbar involvement as an emergency before outpatient electrodiagnostic certainty is complete.
recognize: Myasthenia commonly produces fatigable ocular/bulbar/proximal weakness with preserved sensation.
Lambert-Eaton often causes proximal leg weakness, reduced reflexes and autonomic symptoms with transient facilitation after exercise and may be paraneoplastic.
Botulism can cause descending weakness, cranial neuropathies, autonomic/pupillary findings and respiratory failure.
differentiate: Peripheral neuropathy produces sensory abnormalities; inflammatory myopathy usually has fixed proximal weakness rather than classic fatigability; brainstem stroke is abrupt and focal.
Cholinergic, medication or toxin effects can imitate/worsen junction disease.
assessment: Assess ocular/bulbar symptoms, limb pattern, reflexes, pupils/autonomic features, respiratory effort/cough, medication/toxin/food exposure and cancer risk.
workup: Use antibody/electrodiagnostic testing matched to suspected disorder; assess thymoma for myasthenia and malignancy—especially small-cell lung cancer—when Lambert-Eaton is suspected.
Suspected botulism requires immediate public-health/toxicology/acute-care coordination rather than waiting for routine clinic testing.
management: Treat the specific disorder through neuromuscular specialty care; MG may require pyridostigmine/immunotherapy/thymectomy strategies, LEMS treatment includes cancer management plus symptomatic/immunologic therapy, and botulism requires urgent antitoxin/supportive care.
Respiratory/bulbar compromise requires monitored acute care.
medicationSafety: Magnesium and several antibiotic/cardiac/sedating drugs can worsen neuromuscular transmission; review medications aggressively when weakness worsens.
Do not assume all fluctuating weakness is myasthenia and increase pyridostigmine blindly.
counselling: Teach urgent respiratory/swallowing warning symptoms and provide medication-risk guidance specific to the confirmed disorder.
followUp: Track function, respiratory/bulbar symptoms and underlying cancer/immune treatment response.
examTrap: Calling proximal weakness with dry mouth and absent reflexes 'myasthenia' without considering Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
oneLinePearl: At the neuromuscular junction, pupils, reflexes, autonomic symptoms and exercise response help localize the disorder.

title: Movement Disorders Beyond Parkinson Disease: Describe the Movement Before Naming It
bottomLine: Movement-disorder reasoning starts by describing phenomenology—tremor, chorea, dystonia, tic, myoclonus, ataxia or medication-induced movement—before choosing a disease label. Medication/toxin exposure and time course often provide the fastest diagnostic clue, while abrupt new movement plus other neurologic findings may be an emergency.
recognize: Chorea is irregular flowing movement; dystonia is patterned twisting/posture; myoclonus is brief shock-like movement; tics are stereotyped and often suppressible; ataxia is incoordination rather than involuntary movement.
Antipsychotics/metoclopramide and other dopamine-blocking drugs can cause acute dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia or tardive syndromes.
differentiate: Essential tremor and Parkinson tremor differ from chorea/dystonia; functional movement disorders have positive inconsistency/entrainment features rather than being diagnoses of exclusion alone.
Acute hemiballismus/chorea can be vascular/metabolic and needs cause evaluation.
assessment: Describe body distribution, activation condition, suppressibility, triggers, onset/tempo, medication exposure, family history and accompanying cognitive/psychiatric/cerebellar/neurologic findings.
workup: Testing is phenotype-directed: metabolic/toxic labs, MRI, genetic testing or specialist examination only when the pattern supports them.
Medication-induced syndromes require a detailed exposure/timing history before expensive testing.
management: Treat reversible causes and stop/modify offending drugs when safe; use phenotype-specific therapy and movement-disorder referral for disabling/uncertain disease.
Acute severe dystonia with airway involvement, hyperthermia/rigidity or rapidly evolving neurologic deficits requires emergency management.
medicationSafety: VMAT2 inhibitors, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines and dopamine-modifying drugs have substantial psychiatric, sedation, parkinsonism or QT risks and require diagnosis-specific use.
Avoid reflexively adding another dopamine blocker to akathisia/tardive symptoms caused by one.
redFlags: Abrupt focal movement with stroke features
counselling: Use videos when helpful to document episodic movements and teach patients to report new medication-related restlessness, stiffness or involuntary movement early.
followUp: Track function and phenomenology over time; evolving signs may clarify an initially uncertain syndrome.
examTrap: Calling every tremor or abnormal movement Parkinson disease before describing what the movement actually is.
oneLinePearl: Name the movement first; the disease name comes second.
sourceBasis: Parkinson Canada differential and medication resources

title: Neurologic Manifestations of Systemic Disease: Localize Before Calling It Primary Neurology
bottomLine: Neurologic symptoms can be the first sign of endocrine, metabolic, infectious, autoimmune, malignant, hepatic/renal, nutritional or medication/toxic disease. Localize the neurologic syndrome, then look for systemic context and reversible physiology instead of assuming every neuropathy, seizure, weakness or cognitive change is a primary neurologic disorder.
recognize: Hypoglycemia/electrolyte disorders can cause seizure/confusion; hepatic/uremic disease can cause encephalopathy; thyroid/B12/diabetes can produce cognitive/neuromuscular syndromes; autoimmune/infectious/cancer disease can affect CNS/PNS.
Medication toxicity and withdrawal are common, reversible neurologic mimics.
differentiate: Focal sudden deficits remain stroke emergencies even when systemic illness is present.
Diffuse symmetric metabolic/toxic encephalopathy differs from a focal cortical syndrome, but severe systemic disease can coexist with stroke/seizure.
assessment: Localize: cortex, brainstem/cerebellum, spinal cord, root, peripheral nerve, neuromuscular junction or muscle; then assess tempo, systemic symptoms, medications, toxins, nutrition, pregnancy and organ dysfunction.
workup: Use high-yield physiologic tests—glucose, electrolytes, renal/hepatic function, CBC/B12/thyroid, infection/toxin testing—only as supported by the phenotype and acuity.
Imaging/CSF/electrodiagnostics are driven by localization and red flags rather than a generic neurologic panel.
management: Stabilize and correct time-sensitive systemic causes while treating neurologic complications such as seizure or cerebral edema through the appropriate acute pathway.
Refer persistent focal, inflammatory, paraneoplastic or diagnostically uncertain syndromes for specialty evaluation.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic failure can cause accumulation of sedatives, gabapentinoids, opioids and other neuroactive drugs.
Abrupt withdrawal of alcohol/benzodiazepines/antiseizure drugs can itself create neurologic emergencies.
counselling: Explain when the neurologic symptom is likely being driven by a systemic condition and why treating the systemic cause is part of neurologic care.
followUp: Confirm neurologic recovery as the systemic disorder improves; persistent deficits require re-localization and alternate diagnosis review.
examTrap: Ordering extensive neurologic testing for confusion before checking glucose, sodium, medications, renal/hepatic failure and infection.
oneLinePearl: Localize the nervous-system problem, then ask what systemic disease could be driving it.
